chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
title: Jelly Roll's character and the Princeton prom
summary: Dance and Caldwell on Jelly's braggadocio and kindness; at a Princeton June prom Jelly Roll announced himself as king of jazz to students.

bands.name: Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Oh, he really -- well, you know, people always say that he was another braggadocio, but then other people say he was a very nice guy.
He was. He was a beautiful guy to work for. But he'd make you mad, because the things he would do not intentionally, but that was just the way he was.
Yeah, he was really a sort of big mouth at times.
Yeah, we played player for the June prom

dance at Princeton University out at Princeton, New Jersey, Jelly at the piano was there, and Jelly (unintelligible) Martin and his Hot Peppers and so and so and so. You know how the students are. So they drink. Well, after we had intermission, say, hey, I want to know who is this guy Jelly Roll Martin. So we said, the piano player. Well, these students are funny, you know. They walk up and say, hey, Mr. Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll said, yeah. This is me (unintelligible), the king of the jazz, this was the jingle of the jazz. And I said, is that what you call yourself? (Unintelligible).
He said, this is me, Jelly Roll, said, well, you ain't nothing. Oh, no (unintelligible).

Jelly got (unintelligible). I'm the only one, and got up, said, let me show you what I'm going to play. And, oh, Lord, that was it. I said, Jelly, you aren't going to never learn, are you. He wouldn't take my word because he used to catch it sometimes when he was talking about (unintelligible), but I remember a thing, what he thought he remembered, but it wasn't accurate. So I tell him, said, that's wrong. I said so and so and so.
He said, hey, (unintelligible) fellow, how do you know so much? Well, I was born -- I should know.
But he was a fine guy to work with, beautiful.
